new_statements.quote: Primary word stress is strictly word-initial in BK; since all affixation in this language is suffixal, primary word stress falls on the root; e.g. bə́ʈʈə 'mountain', úpeːlgən 'crow pheasant', t̪óɖŋgiṣəɖə 'began to V'. Further research is necessary to provide an accurate description of secondary stress; however, the following points may be mentioned at this point in my description: In words with lexical suffixes (these suffixes are derived from roots), the lexical suffix bears secondary stress on its initial syllable; [...] In compound words, the leftmost member of the compound bears primary stress on its initial syllable, and later members bear secondary stress on their initial syllables; [...] All word-final vowels are unstressed. (pp. 255-256)

Further research is necessary to provide an accurate description of secondary stress; however, the following points may be mentioned at this point in my descripti…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress always falls on the first syllable of the word, which is the first syllable of the root because all affixes are suffixes. The word-initial syllable is 'always assigned primary stress' (p. 245). No weight or lexical conditioning is mentioned for primary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Provisional (author says further research needed): the initial syllable of a lexical suffix (suffixes derived from roots, e.g. /-aːɭ/, /-əɖi/) bears secondary stress; in compounds the first member has primary stress on its initial syllable and later members bear secondary stress on their initial syllables (áɖkmèri 'arecanut tree' from áɖki + méri). Secondary stress in other medial syllables 'appears to be dependent on vowel quality and length'. /ə/ is unstressed in medial syllables unless suffix- or compound-initial. All word-final vowels are unstressed.
new_statements.exceptions: None for primary stress. Monomoraic pronouns are noted as sub-minimal words (p. 255) but no stress exception is stated for them.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word including suffixes and compounds); examples are isolated citation forms marked with acute (primary) and grave (secondary) accents. IPA example glyphs in the quote were transcribed from the rendered page image (PDF pp. 270-271) because the PDF text layer uses a private-use IPA font.
new_statements.identity_note: Coelho 2003 describes Betta Kurumba ('BK') as spoken in the Gudalur area of the Nilgiris (Tamil Nadu) — the language-level bett1235 itself; no sub-dialect is singled out. The earlier scan's note of a 'Brill 2018 revision' of the grammar is inaccurate: Brill 2018 is a text collection (Annotated Texts in Beṭṭa Kurumba), and the 2019 Routledge chapter is the published sketch. Jayapaul 1978 and Upadhyaya 1972 ('Kurumba'/'Kuruba') may describe other Kurumba varieties.

sources.note: Chapter 6 Phonology, section 2.4 'Stress', pp. 255-256: primary word stress is strictly word-initial (on the root, since all affixation is suffixal); lexical suffixes and non-initial compound members bear secondary stress on their initial syllable; medial secondary stress possibly vowel-quality/length dependent (further research needed); schwa unstressed medially except suffix/compound-initial; all word-final vowels unstressed. Also p. 245 (section 1.2 Vowels): the word-initial syllable 'is always assigned primary stress'. Obtained from the Wayback Machine capture (2016-03-03) of the original…
